summary: Aims to extend the security features of IPsec to remote access users who dial in over the Internet, using L2TP. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: People dialing in from afar should have protection too. This explains how to wrap their private pipe in a lock.

questions: how does l2tp provide secure remote access
what is a secure remote access server
how do you configure l2tp and ipsec for dial-in users
why merge the nAS and security gateway
subtitle: Secure dial-in from the Internet using L2TP tunneling and IPsec encryption

tldr.problem: Enterprises want to allow employees to dial in over the Internet instead of dedicated phone lines, but the Internet is not trusted. Separate security gateways and NAS servers make it hard to manage users and track sessions. Combining them into one system using L2TP and IPsec lets enterprises mandate encryption for every remote-access packet.
tldr.mechanism: The Secure Remote Access Server (SRAS) merges the functions of a PPP termination server (LNS) with an IPsec security gateway. RADIUS configures per-user security policies. All IP packets embedded in PPP are required to use either AH or ESP encryption, enforced by the SRAS before they enter the enterprise.
tldr.outcome: Remote access over the Internet becomes practical with transparent security: users dial in using PPP, the SRAS handles L2TP and IPsec automatically. The enterprise controls authentication and authorization via RADIUS, with security policies enforced at the gateway rather than trusting intermediate networks.

facts.label: Main advantage
facts.value: Unified RADIUS control of authentication and security

facts.label: Required protocols
facts.value: L2TP for tunneling, IPsec for encryption

today: RFC 2888 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. L2TP with IPsec for remote access remains a deployment model, though modern VPN solutions often use different protocols like IPsec directly or TLS-based approaches.

sections.title: Remote Access Over the Internet
sections.content:
Traditionally, employees dial in to the enterprise via PSTN (the phone network), which is trusted. The dial-in box (NAS) authenticates the user, assigns an IP address via RADIUS, and tracks the session. As the Internet became ubiquitous, businesses wanted to use it for dial-in access to save on phone charges and dedicated lines.

But the Internet is untrusted. A packet crossing the Internet can be eavesdropped, modified or stolen. For a dial-in session to be safe, every packet must be encrypted and authenticated. Traditional firewalls restrict external access to internal resources, but they cannot screen packets from remote dial-in users if those users have an IP address inside the network.

This memo proposes using L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) to carry PPP sessions across the Internet to a security gateway, where IPsec (IP Security) is applied to enforce encryption and authentication. The key insight is merging the NAS and security gateway into a single system.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone called in from the phone network, you did not worry much about someone listening. Now people dial in from the Internet, which is full of eavesdroppers, so you need a lock on every packet.

sections.title: L2TP Architecture and Components
sections.content:
L2TP extends PPP across an IP network. The dial-in client connects to a Local Access Concentrator (LAC), a device near the user (perhaps at an Internet cafe or the user's ISP). The LAC establishes an L2TP tunnel to the L2TP Network Server (LNS), which is the actual dial-in server in the enterprise.

The tunnel carries PPP session data. From the client's perspective, it is dialing into the LNS directly. L2TP uses control messages to set up and tear down tunnels and sessions, separate from the data messages that carry PPP packets. The L2TP header includes a session ID that identifies which user the PPP packet belongs to.

Inside the PPP session, the client negotiates IP parameters and receives an IP address from the LNS. The IP packets carrying user traffic are embedded in PPP, wrapped in L2TP headers, and sent across the Internet to the LNS.
sections.plainLanguage: The client connects to a convenient dial-in box near them (the LAC). That box tunnels the connection through the Internet to the real corporate dial-in server (the LNS). To the user, it looks like a normal dial-in.

sections.title: Enterprise Security Requirements and Trust Model
sections.content:
Enterprises protect their networks with firewalls and place external servers in a demilitarized zone (DMZ). Internal resources are off-limits to the Internet. This model breaks down for dial-in access: if remote users get an IP address inside the corporate network, firewall rules that block external access no longer apply.

The solution is a Security Gateway (SGW) that uses IPsec to authenticate and encrypt all traffic from remote users. Only packets from authenticated, encrypted sources are allowed into the enterprise network. The gateway is placed behind the firewall so the firewall can be configured to allow only L2TP and IKE (key exchange) traffic.

However, placing the SGW separately from the LNS creates problems: the SGW does not know when a user session ends (so it cannot clean up security associations), and packets might not traverse both devices in both directions. Merging them into a single Secure Remote Access Server (SRAS) solves these issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The firewall trusts nothing from the Internet. The dial-in server can let anyone in. You need a security check in between: a box that decrypts the dial-in packets, checks that they are from a real user, and only then lets them into the network.

sections.title: The Secure Remote Access Server (SRAS)
sections.content:
The SRAS combines the LNS (PPP termination point) and IPsec security gateway into one system. It receives L2TP packets from the Internet, extracts the PPP session, and checks that the IP packets embedded in PPP are either AH (Authentication Header) or ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) packets directed to the SRAS itself. Non-IPsec packets are dropped.

The SRAS also accepts IKE (UDP port 500) packets for key negotiation, allowing dynamic IPsec security associations. When the PPP session ends, the SRAS cleans up the associated IPsec and IKE security associations.

RADIUS configuration is leveraged for security: new RADIUS attributes specify whether IPsec is mandatory for the user, reference security profiles that define access control filters and encryption preferences, and can point to IKE negotiation parameters for automated key exchange. This way, the enterprise uses a single RADIUS database to manage both authentication and security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: One box handles everything: receives dial-in calls, checks that each packet is encrypted properly, assigns IP addresses from RADIUS, and cleans up when the user hangs up.

sections.title: RADIUS Attributes for Security Configuration
sections.content:
Three new RADIUS attributes enable SRAS configuration. IPSEC_MANDATE specifies whether IPsec is required (0 = no, 1 = required for LNS only, 2 = required for any NAS). SECURITY_PROFILE references a file with access control policies and encryption preferences. IKE_NEGOTIATION_PROFILE references a file with IKE credentials and negotiation parameters for dynamic key exchange.

The IPSEC_MANDATE attribute is crucial: it tells the NAS to drop any non-IPsec IP packets in the PPP session (except IKE negotiation). This enforces the security policy transparently without requiring the user to manually configure IPsec on their machine (though users can choose to add an additional layer of IPsec if they wish).

The ability to assign security profiles on a per-user basis via RADIUS centralizes the configuration burden and leverages existing AAA infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The dial-in box looks at RADIUS to see if this user must use encryption. If yes, it rejects any unencrypted packets. The RADIUS database can also point to a security rule file that says which networks this user can reach.

sections.title: Limitations and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The SRAS model has several limitations. First, tunneling overhead: L2TP headers plus IPsec headers plus PPP headers add significant overhead to each packet, reducing throughput and potentially requiring fragmentation and reassembly.

Second, users may need to authenticate twice: once to the LCP (Link Control Protocol) for dial-in, and again to IKE for key exchange. The memo suggests using Extended Authentication Protocol (EAP) to unify these, but that adds complexity.

Third, LCP (the dial-in protocol) sends usernames and passwords in the clear across the Internet. An attacker could steal credentials and impersonate a user, though the SRAS will drop non-IPsec packets so the attacker cannot access the network. Using EAP or IPsec for LCP itself mitigates this, but requires more infrastructure.

Finally, the SRAS computational overhead for IPsec processing on all remote-user packets can be a bottleneck for high-scale deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: The approach works, but it is expensive in overhead, requires users to authenticate twice sometimes, and exposes passwords during the dial-in phase. Better security requires more complexity.
